query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under demanding mechanical loading (high strain rates and service-relevant temperatures), an initially homogeneous, single‐phase HEA undergoes stress‐activated local compositional segregation and nano‐precipitation. These microstructural evolutions inhibit dislocation motion and reduce the effective slip distance, thereby triggering a loss in toughness and a shift toward brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase solid solution high‐entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure and high ductility/toughness.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled mechanical loading with systematically varied strain rates and temperatures in a service-relevant regime while performing in situ high-resolution microstructural characterization.
generation.conditions: Strain rates ranging from quasi-static (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) to high (≈10²–10³ s⁻¹) and temperatures from room temperature up to moderately elevated service conditions (e.g., up to 1073 K), representative of harsh engineering environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Stress-induced formation of nano-scale precipitates or local phase segregation at high local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: Under high mechanical load, local energy fluctuations promote phase instability in the uniform solid solution, leading to the nucleation of nano-precipitates. These precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation slip, reducing ductility and toughness, and ultimately facilitating brittle fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: In comparison to the baseline homogeneous state, the loaded samples will exhibit the onset of nano-precipitation or compositional segregation at specific critical strain rates and temperatures, accompanied by a measurable drop in toughness, a shift in fracture morphology (from ductile dimpled to brittle cleavage), and changes in the strain hardening behavior.
generation.baseline: The initial as-cast, single-phase HEA exhibiting uniform microstructure with high toughness and ductile failure under similar mechanical tests.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to manifest within service conditions where mechanical loading induces sufficient localized stress, but not at temperatures high enough to completely re-homogenize the structure. Deviations outside the defined strain rate and temperature boundaries may not trigger the phase evolution.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold strain rate and temperature at which the nano-precipitation initiates and the quantitative impact on toughness are not yet determined; the mechanism may also depend on subtle compositional factors unique to different HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-energy X-ray diffraction combined with digital image correlation on HEA specimens subjected to a range of controlled strain rates and temperatures. Simultaneously monitor the evolution of nano-scale precipitates or compositional fluctuations alongside mechanical property measurements (e.g., toughness and strain hardening rate).
measurements: Temporal evolution of phase fractions and nano-precipitate size/distribution
Stress-strain curves and strain hardening rate measurements
Fractography analysis to discern brittle versus ductile fracture modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under service-like loading conditions there is no detectable onset of nano-precipitation or local phase segregation correlated with a significant reduction in toughness (i.e., if the HEA retains its ductile fracture characteristics and uniform microstructure), then the hypothesis of stress-induced microstructural evolution causing embrittlement is falsified.

The bright-field TEM image in Fig. 2a demonstrates that the alloy is composed of an fcc matrix in which the hcp phase grows in the form of laminate with a thickness ranging from several to several hundred nanometers. High-resolution HAADF-STEM images of the hcp phase were taken along the fcc [110] direction (Fig. 2b), from which the coherent phase boundaries between the fcc and hcp phases can be observed. The interphase plane is represented by the close-packed planes of each structure: (111) for the fcc and (0001) for the hcp phase. No crystal defects, such as dislocations could be observed at these phase boundaries. Compared to other single-phase HEAs, the microstructure of this DP-HEA is significantly more complex. The hcp phase grows in the fcc matrix and, as such, serves to terminate slip planes for dislocation glide, thereby reducing the mean-free path for dislocation glide. AbstractIn this study, we manufactured a non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 high-entropy alloy (HEA) consisting of a single-phase face-centered-cubic structure. We applied in situ neutron diffraction coupled with electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to investigate its tensile properties, microstructural evolution, lattice strains and texture development, and the stacking fault energy. The non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 HEA revealed a good combination of strength and ductility in mechanical properties compared to the equiatomic CoNiCrFe HEA, due to both stable solid solution and precipitation-strengthened effects. The non-equiatomic stoichiometry resulted in not only a lower electronegativity mismatch, indicating a more stable state of solid solution, but also a higher stacking fault energy (SFE, ~50 mJ/m2) due to the higher amount of Ni and the lower amount of Cr. This higher SFE led to a more active motion of dislocations relative to mechanical twinning, resulting in severe lattice distortion near the grain boundaries and dislocation entanglement near the twin boundaries. decision.trend: Early HEA studies initially established that the single‐phase solid solution can evolve under external loads or thermal exposure into a microstructure that no longer exhibits the originally desired ductile behavior. For example, work on refractory HEAs (PMC10708198) revealed that trace interstitials can promote phase segregation during aging, thereby softening the alloy, while studies on non‐equiatomic single‐phase alloys (PMC8875034) provided evidence that subtle compositional shifts and local instabilities (such as a change in stacking fault energy) can locally alter the deformation mode – shifting from homogeneous plasticity to mechanisms that favor cracking. The progression has been from bulk post‐mortem and phenomenological characterizations toward more microstructure‐sensitive analyses. Nonetheless, no study has yet dynamically connected the onset of microstructural evolution (such as nano‐precipitation, stress‐induced phase segregation, or local compositional fluctuations) during service‐relevant loading with the concomitant loss of toughness or induction of brittle fracture.
decision.unsolved: The critical unsolved issue remains identifying and quantifying the precise microstructural transition that causes the HEA to lose its ductility – that is, a direct, testable mechanistic link between dynamic stress/temperature conditions and the triggering of localized phase transformations or segregation that lead to brittle failure. In other words, although prior work hints at roles for nano‐precipitates, local compositional fluctuations, or stress‐assisted phase decomposition, a controlled, in situ comparison that ties these changes quantitatively to the drop in toughness is still missing.
decision.lever: Systematically vary strain rate and temperature in service-relevant regimes while performing in situ high-resolution microstructural characterization (e.g., time-resolved high-energy X-ray diffraction and digital image correlation) to detect the onset/kinetics of nano-precipitation or phase segregation relative to the undisturbed single-phase baseline.
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend from post-mortem analyses towards dynamic measurements: it will reveal the precise stress/temperature boundaries where microstructural evolution correlates with toughness loss, thereby providing the needed falsifiable benchmark — if no microstructural change is observed as the toughness drops, the proposed mechanism would be ruled out.
